title: The Letter to the Galatians
lead: Galatians is Paul's angry, passionate letter to churches he had founded in Galatia, written because other teachers were telling his Gentile converts that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. It argues that Gentiles are already children of Abraham through faith in Christ and the gift of the Spirit, and it is the letter on which Luther, and many after him, built the teaching of justification by faith.

sections.b: After a greeting with no thanks and a curse on anyone who preaches another good news (1:1-10), Paul tells how he received the good news and how the Jerusalem leaders accepted it, ending with his open clash with Cephas at Antioch (1:11-2:21). He then argues from the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit and from the story of Abraham that the law cannot give life or make a family (3:1-4:31), urges them to stand in freedom and to live by the Spirit in love (5:1-6:10), and closes in his own hand with a last warning (6:11-18).

The letter is read as the charter of Protestant teaching on faith and works, as a Jewish-Christian argument about whether non-Jews must become Jews, and as a letter that has sometimes been turned against Jews. Scholars and churches differ over what Paul means by 'works of the law', over 'the faith of Christ', and over his words about Hagar and Sarah and 'the Israel of God'.
